title: Tom Brown's music store and bringing jazz north
summary: A caller remembers Tom Brown's store; Allen lists his recordings, and Wiggs says Brown's band was first white band to take jazz to Chicago and New York; a caller asks about song markets.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Good morning. I heard Tom Brown's name mentioned, and I recall when I was a boy, and that goes back in the 20s, he operated a music supply store on a magazine near Jackson Avenue. He and his wife, do you recall that? Yeah, I remember.
You just heard him on records, too. When the Saints go marching in, he was on, and he was on Ole Miss.

Yeah, well, I miss the earlier part, yes. And I used to go there. I took violin when I was a youngster. I'd go there, you know, get the strings. And I used to love to go in there. It was sort of, you know, it had a real nice atmosphere about it. Well, you're welcome.

Well, he's one of the great New Orleans trombonists, recording, of course, with Johnny in the 50s, and he dates back long before that. One of his prize records from the 20s was made with Johnny Barsdorfer. Oh. And he recorded also with a band that Johnny Wiggs just mentioned, Norman Brownlee's orchestra. And I couldn't begin to talk about Tom Brown's recordings. There's so many of them he recorded in New York. He was up there quite early.

Yeah, he caught it raw. He was on Canal Street. I remember that. It should be known that Tom Brown was the first white man to take jazz out of New Orleans, his band. Oh, yeah. Up to Chicago, yeah. Up to Chicago, yeah. All the way up there, and then on to New York. That's where they call him that dirty old name of a jazz player. Before getting off, I wanted to ask you, since I'm in my 50s, too, I mean, I do a little composing, but I can't adapt to rock and roll. Perhaps I'm too old. But is there any market for songs, you know, more or less in the ballad or semi-jazz type? If you're Leo Feist's son, a son-in-law maybe. I don't know whether you know Leo Feist. I've heard up in New York. He used to, when I was in New York about 300 years ago, he used to put out, he was the biggest publisher in New York. But I've got a trunk full of things which I can't do anything with unless I'm on my own recording session. Oh, I see, yeah. Then I can use it. I stuff it down the band's throat, you know, and they have no chance.
